articles.title: Polyend releases the Tracker firmware source code
articles.content: Polyend releases the Tracker firmware source code Today we’re publishing the firmware source code for the original Tracker, Tracker+ and Tracker Mini on GitHub. We’re also releasing Tracker Community Edition 1.0 with tons of new features and improvements. You can install it on any of the three instruments, modify the firmware yourself and share your own version. We’ve built in a recovery system to keep a faulty firmware build from bricking your Tracker. Explore the Tracker Community Edition repository on GitHub Here at Polyend, creativity is what we value most. We’ve seen it firsthand in the unofficial Tracker mods you’ve built, and we’re sharing the firmware source code to support that work. Maybe you want to build an entirely new instrument on the Tracker hardware. Or maybe there’s just one thing you wish your Tracker did differently. Either way, you can now try it on the unit you already own. I bet some of you already have ideas for the original Tracker that never crossed our minds. Piotr Raczyński, CEO of Polyend What’s new in Community Edition 1.0 Stream long samples from the SD card. Bring full-length stems, loops and field recordings into a project using a fraction of the sample memory they’d normally need. This works even on the original Tracker. Record timing and velocity while keeping both step FX slots free. Micro-move and Volume now have dedicated fields on every step. New Chance conditions let you bring in a snare fill every fourth pass. Load plugins in the Sample Editor. Six effects and generators are included, from an analog-style kick generator to a stereo delay. The plugin SDK lets you build, share and sell your own. Play two new synths on Tracker+ and Tracker Mini. CHIP and DIRT join the synth lineup. A new SDK lets you build your own synth engines. All three models also get wavetable envelopes and LFOs, faster project loading and saving, and tighter MIDI clock timing. You can design custom Tracker themes and fonts in your browser.
articles.summary: Polyend 在 GitHub 开源 Tracker 系列固件源码，并发布社区版 1.0，含大量新功能。

articles.title: Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen
articles.content: TL;DR We find that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights , well past what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms. This might be a big deal for both optimization and interpretability. Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming . Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights . Read Which game was this neural network trained on? Astra reads the 17,253 weights, with no tools Breakout 99% confident Fix A trained policy never gets the car over the strip. Astra edits 3.5% of the weights, in one shot 100% success, up from 0% Improve Make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math. Astra edits the weights in a Python kernel, with no training 48.1% on MATH-500, up from 7.9% If you were asked to handcraft a neural network that plays Go, what would you do? If you were handed raw neural network weights and asked to predict their behavior, where would you even start? For almost any human, this is practically impossible. Today, weights are written by optimization , by custom networks trained to write them , or by compilers from formal programs . In this post, we find that the current generation of frontier LLMs, used natively in natural language, are starting to become eerily good at understanding and crafting neural network weights around natural-language goals. Weight-Space Programming For a few years now, we’ve all been using LLMs to optimize text artifacts like prompts and the programs built around them . More recently, we’ve started using them to optimize whole harnesses and the training code and hyperparameters that train ML models . We often justified these methods by reference to the fact that we don’t know other principled ways to hill-climb on text artifacts, unlike for updating the weights of differentiable neural networks . After all, humans can “optimize” code by hand, for example, so it made sense to ask LLMs to do it, but they can’

articles.title: If you love a website, back it up
articles.content: This story starts with a little tragedy. See, I’ve got these old webpages I love to go back and look on every now and then. There’s websites that have been online unchanged for years and years, or decades, and there’s something a little cozy about checking in on them every now and then to see an old friend is still doing okay. Sometimes, of course, tragedy strikes. There was this fansite called teapuppies.com for an old anime series and and toy line called Ochaken . It’s about these cute cartoon dog characters who have tea leaves for ears, each of them named after a different kind of tea. The site had been online since 2004 and had basically not changed since 2005, but it was nice just having it around. Except when I went to visit it a few weeks ago, and discovered that not only was the site gone but the domain is now being used to serve online gambling ads. I work in web archiving, by the way. Which is to say that I should have known the site would go offline someday, and that I have the tools to have done something about it. I could have archived that site while it was still around, but I didn’t. This post is here to beg you to do what I didn’t think to, and to teach you how. You see, when I talk to a lot of people about web archiving, they always seem to believe it’s something they couldn’t do. It’s something a big organization like the Internet Archive does, and if you want a webpage to be saved you just have to wait and hope it gets done. But that’s not true! What I really want everyone to know is that you have control over the world around you, you can take action to preserve things and make things better. And not just can , but should ! Don’t just wait for someone else to act - get out there and and make it happen! Got a favourite site? Back it up! Got some information you don’t want to get lost? Back it up! Favourite post somewhere? All together now. Back! It! Up! All of the tools I’ll be showing off in this post use standard web archiving formats like WARC . You don’t have to worry about any of the technical details , but I’m telling you that because it means there are a lot of really great tools to do whatever you want with them. Here, just as an example, is an entire archived website embedded right in this blog post: You can even click through all the links, look at all of the images, the works. It’s an entire website right in a post! (And if you don’t trust me to keep this up, and you want the web archive to host somewhere else? You can download it for yourself right from there. Just click the kebab menu and choose “download archive”, and you can do whatever you like with it. In fact, please do!) By the way, for disclosure: the tools I’m going to mention in this blog post are made by the company I work for, but that’s not because they’ll pay my salary (most of them are free!). I just happen to think these are the best tools there are for personal web archiving. Option 1 - ArchiveWeb.page browser extension By far the easiest personal w

articles.title: Self-Employed? Solopreneur? NIST Has a Cybersecurity Guide Just for You
articles.content: Credit: Asian Isolated/Shutterstock If you work for yourself, as millions of Americans do, protecting your business from cyberattack is one of many responsibilities that falls entirely on your shoulders. Don’t feel daunted: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has just released a guide with your needs — and busy life — in mind. Small Business Cybersecurity: Non-Employer Firms (NIST Cybersecurity White Paper 50) is a lay-language resource offering cybersecurity basics tailored expressly to the “solopreneur” — a term referring to anyone who is a business’s sole paid employee. More than 28 million small businesses in the U.S. fall into the solopreneur category, existing in every industry and forming a substantial part of the economy. The publication is written to introduce solopreneurs to the fundamentals of a small-business cybersecurity program and provide an actionable approach to implementing it. “Because solopreneurs may not have cybersecurity expertise, we wanted to create a resource designed for them,” said NIST’s Daniel Eliot, one of the publication’s authors. “They can implement many of these actions on their own with limited technical knowledge or with minimal financial investment.” The publication is an update to what was previously titled Small Business Information Security: The Fundamentals ( NISTIR 7621 ). While that publication was aimed at small businesses of varying sizes and covered the broader topic of information security, the revision is narrower in scope and concentrates on protecting digital systems from malicious attack. The updated publication draws its guidelines from the well-known NIST Cybersecurity Framework ( CSF 2.0 ), though the new publication is written with the novice in mind. “This publication assumes the reader has no familiarity with cybersecurity or the NIST CSF,” Eliot said. “We want to educate people about what cybersecurity is and how it fits in with a successful business plan. We know solopreneurs are often very busy people, so any time we introduce a topic or throw out jargony terms, we try to provide context and definitions for the lay reader.” The publication’s opening section, which includes the introduction and a chapter on the NIST CSF, is essentially a primer on cybersecurity and how it can support a solopreneur’s business. “In addition to the general context, we highlight a set of actionable best practices that significantly reduce cybersecurity risks. These include regular data backups and maintaining updated software,” Eliot said. “They are a good set of first steps a small business might take.” The central section offers specific actions from the CSF that can be implemented in a solo business. For each of these actions, the guide includes the rationale for performing it, how the business can get started, and options for what to do later as the business grows. Each action offers a brief citation that maps to the relevant section in the CSF and often references additional resou
articles.summary: NIST 发布面向自由职业者和个体创业者的网络安全指南，帮助其防范网络攻击。

articles.title: Intel stock collapse worsens as $3.5T chip rout spreads
articles.content: Wall Street mostly swept up last week's tech wreckage Monday. Chip stocks kept tracking mud back through the house. About 7 in 10 S&P 500 stocks rose Monday, yet nearly every chip stock fell, and the group shed more than $400 billion in market value in a single session, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Intel ( INTC ) led the way down again. 59.97 -5.79 (-8.80%) At close: November 2 at 4:00:01 PM EST 60.81 +0.84 (+1.40%) Overnight: 10:53:34 PM EST The chipmaker slid about 9% after its worst day since 1974 on Oct. 30, when a disappointing forecast knocked nearly 29% off the stock. Monday's close left Intel worth less than half of what it was when September ended. And the damage didn't stick to Intel. Micron ( MU ), Sandisk ( SNDK ), Seagate ( STX ), and Western Digital ( WDC ) — the memory and storage names that led the chip boom this year — all got clobbered, falling roughly 6% to 8%. Marvell ( MRVL ) fell even harder, a drop that came as it agreed to buy Lumentum ( LITE ) in a $115 billion deal. Nvidia ( NVDA ) held up better than most, but it's still down about 16% since Oct. 6. Intel, Marvell, AMD and the memory names led the chip rout, while Nvidia barely moved. · Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace Zoom out and the mess gets bigger. Chip and memory stocks have lost about $3.7 trillion in market value since Oct. 6, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Nvidia lost the most in dollars, but Intel's drop of nearly half is the steepest among the giants. Yahoo Finance Not everything tied to AI bled. SpaceX ( SPCX ) rose, though it's still well below where it started October. Software was mixed, apart from cybersecurity stocks like Fortinet ( FTNT ) and CrowdStrike ( CRWD ), which fell with chips. Adam Johnson, founder of the Bullseye Brief and portfolio manager of the American Ingenuity Fund, thinks last week's sell-off already priced in the worst. "The market kitchen-sinked it," Johnson told Yahoo Finance on Monday. "They discounted everything that could go wrong. And when you do that, typically that's when you see a bottom." John Chambers, founder and CEO of JC2 Ventures and Cisco's former CEO, expects the gap between winners and losers to keep widening. "There will be major train wrecks," Chambers told Yahoo Finance, also on Monday. "And rising tide does not raise all boats. I would not bet against Nvidia." Stock Trader's Almanac editor Jeff Hirsch, who coined the term " Octoberphobia ," bought the sell-off on Oct. 30. History is on his side. Chips have climbed in all eight midterm cycles since 1994, measured from the last October close through the following June, by Yahoo Finance calculations. But in 2002 and 2018, they first fell about another 11%. Next up is AMD ( AMD ), which reports third quarter results Tuesday after the bell , the same day as the midterm vote.
articles.summary: 芯片股集体大跌，单日市值蒸发超 4000 亿美元，英特尔股价跌势进一步加剧。

articles.title: The SEC Should Block Anthropic's IPO to Protect the Public
articles.content: Matt Scherer is co-author of the recent report Brace for Impact: Protecting people and the economy when the AI bubble bursts . Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei looks on as United States President Donald Trump holds a press briefing with AI executives following a meeting on artificial intelligence, outside the West Wing of the White House on September 29, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images) Things are seldom what they seem when it comes to the finances of the AI industry. The AI ecosystem’s circular business dealings , extensive use of financial engineering , and otherwise murky finances make it hard for investors, regulators, or workers saving for retirement to get an accurate financial picture of AI companies. That is particularly true of Anthropic, which filed the registration statement for its initial public offering (IPO) last week ahead of a planned November stock market debut. The company’s topline financial figures look quite impressive for a startup, with revenues that appear to have grown quickly over the course of 2026 and a fairly healthy balance sheet — on the surface, that is. Dig a little deeper, however, and a far bleaker picture emerges. Footnotes to the company’s most recent financial disclosures revealed nearly $900 billion in spending commitments, most of them stretching into the 2030s. The company’s financial results for 2026 have not been subjected to formal auditing, which makes them less-than-reliable, but the third-quarter results suggest that the company’s revenue growth slowed to a crawl over the summer. Anthropic will have to reverse that trend and sustain extraordinary revenue growth to meet its vast obligations. But the financial pressures that are squeezing Anthropic — and, indeed, the AI industry as a whole — will make it exceptionally hard for the leading model developer to do so. If the company goes public, workers, retail investors, and retirees will increasingly be left holding the bag when Anthropic’s bills come due. The financial mountain that Anthropic must climb is unprecedented for a company making its stock market debut. While Anthropic has an impressive $96 billion in cash reserves, its amended registration statement reveals at least $582 billion in non-cancelable spending commitments to just five companies (Amazon, AMD, Broadcom, Google, and Microsoft) to gain access to the vast computational power required to train and run Anthropic’s generative AI models. Even though they do not appear on Anthropic’s balance sheet, those obligations are effectively debts in a legal and practical sense : they are payments that Anthropic is contractually required to make in the future, regardless of whether the company can afford to do so. Moreover, it is not clear how much of the remaining $300 billion or so of the $895 billion in contractual commitments will ultimately land on Anthropic’s balance sheet. With the company continuing to negotiate further massive infrastructure and compute contracts , A

articles.title: Jailbreaking my car's navigation system just so I can change the time
articles.content: The car that I drive is a 2014 Renault Latitude. It's not a fancy car by any means and is starting to show its age, but it gets me from point A to point B and does everything else reasonably well so I've never really had any reason to complain. When I bought the car, the previous owner asked me whether I wanted a "navigation map SD card" with it. They mentioned that the car apparently needs this SD card just to change the time on the clock, but I didn't really find that believable - not that they were lying to me, but perhaps they couldn't figure out how to enter the correct settings menu. After all, videos of similar head units online showed the menu with the clock settings option right there. Since the maps on the SD card were apparently very out of date and didn't function properly, I decided I didn't need it and the previous owner tossed it. I didn't really miss it. The dashboard display did show a large "No maps found!" message taking up the majority of the display, but it didn't bother me too much. Like most other European countries, Estonia uses daylight saving time, and we recently switched from summer time (UTC+3) to "winter time" (UTC+2), which meant that the time displayed on the dashboard was out of sync by an hour. I dived into the settings menu, hoping to easily find the "Set time" option in there. That never happened. The menu where the "Set time" option should've been simply didn't have that option. I compared the menus with the ones in online videos, and the option was simply missing. There were two "Settings" buttons on the dash, and one of them worked but only let me change various Bluetooth and phonebook settings, with no time & date settings in sight. The second Settings button did not work whatsoever, instead showing a "No maps detected!" pop up message every time I pressed it. I must've spent an hour going through various menus, pressing various buttons or button combinations hoping to land in the correct menu, searching the web for information on this particular unit simply because I refused to believe that there was no option to change the time and I clearly must've been missing something obvious . Still in denial, I decided to fetch the firmware and dig into it, hoping to find some indication on how to open the correct settings menu. Luckily, I wasn't the first to embark on this journey and someone had already done some reverse engineering work on this particular unit ( https://github.com/andronedev/carminat-tomtom-live-re/blob/main/README.md ). While it was in French and seemingly heavily LLM-assisted, it did point me to the correct URLs for fetching the update files themselves. When extracted, the update files included a ttsystem file which turned out to be an ext3 filesystem containing the device's root filesystem, which was pretty much exactly what I was looking for. The unit itself (TomTom Carminat LIVE, codename beaumont ) is built around a Samsung S5P6440 SoC running TomTom's custom OS based on Linux 2.6.28.10. Af
articles.summary: 开发者破解 2014 款雷诺 Latitude 车载导航系统，只为修改系统时间，分享逆向过程。

articles.title: A Decade of Kill Bugs
articles.content: On the morning of September 24th 2026, Endcrawl had a brief outage. I'd just typed: And instantly all services went down. Right away I blamed myself. Maybe I mistyped that number! Maybe my code had a signal handling bug. Maybe I don't understand Unix as well as I think I do. Maybe I'm an idiot! As it turned out, the outage was caused by a bug in kill(1) . This is really surprising. The kill program is 50 years old. Its spec is simple and stable. It's probably exercised a billion times a day. A bug in kill was so surprising that, once I'd found it, I couldn't stop there. I needed to know how this bug came to be, and what had led the programmers so badly astray. When I eventually found the root cause, there was an even bigger surprise. It had led to not just one bug, but a whole series of kill bugs that shipped in Ubuntu 14, 16, 18, 22 and 24 LTS. This post documents a decade of kill bugs, then makes some recommendations. Back to the outage. I scrambled to put the fire out. After that came a surprise second fire. By the end of all this I was pretty demoralized. I was ready to accept that I'd made a dumb mistake and ready to get on with the work day. There was this nagging feeling though… Remember that final scene in Burn After Reading? "What did we learn Palmer?" "I don't know sir." "I don't f**king know either. I guess we learned not to do it again." "Yes sir." "Although I'm f**ked if I know what we did..." What had just happened? Was I about to be hit with a third outage? How could I be sure? An outage not understood is an outage that happens again. That nagging feeling I had was a call to understand. With a sigh, I put all my other work on hold and started a proper post mortem. Let's examine the command that caused the outage: The negative number here is a process group identifier , or pgid for short. A pgid is like a pid, but identifies a group of related processes. By convention, killing a positive number sends a signal to a single process, while killing a negative number signals all processes in that process group. I was attempting to cancel a big Endcrawl 7k test render. A normal person would have killed one of the processes involved and let failures cascade to the others. But killing the whole group simultaneously strikes me as cleaner. Process group signaling isn't some exotic operation. You use it all the time. Every time you ^C a command, the tty sends SIGINT to the foreground process group. Interactive shells run all but the simplest commands in a new process group, which among other things makes job control possible. Process group signaling is in fact an awesome Unix innovation. I love it so much I added it to daemontools , where svc -+h now avoids orphans in a multiprocess service bounce. At any rate, imagine my surprise when the command didn't just kill those render processes, but killed all processes on the machine save one! Here's the relevant snippet from procps 4.0.4 , the provider of /bin/kill in Ubuntu 24.04 LTS. Can you spot t

articles.title: An outsider's perspective on Scion and Mononoke
articles.content: An outsider’s perspective on Scion and Mononoke Recently, Anthropic wrote a blog post about their new centralized version control system Scion . As someone working on the Source Control team at Databricks, where we have a huge monorepo and are exploring different options, I figured it might be useful to share my perspective here. (Obligatory disclaimer: This post represents my own views, not my employer’s.) I recommend reading Anthropic’s post before continuing to read this one. You may also want to pre-read Rain Paharia’s Anthropic’s Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke and the follow-up More on Anthropic’s Scion ripping off Mononoke . My history with version control Before we get into the weeds, it might be helpful to you to know where I’m coming from. If you’re not interested in this, you can jump to the Technical Commentary section. I have never worked at Facebook, but one of my all-time favorite tech talks is Durham Goode’s Scaling Mercurial at Facebook from Git Merge 2017. Goode was the longest-serving and most senior member on Facebook’s Source Control team. ( source ) The talk covers various interesting aspects for both the server side and the client side. For the server side, some of the topics include solving push contention with server-side rebasing (pushrebase), using scalable object storage for commits, moving various source control queries to the server, etc. For the client, there’s mention of the smartlog and other CLI commands for easier manipulation of history (compared to rebasing in Git). However, more so than the technical aspects of the talk (which are interesting in their own right!), the main thing that has stayed with me throughout these years is the deep care for users that is reflected in Goode’s tone and words. It’s a bit difficult to convey this without the power of voice, You should watch the presentation! but here are some quotes which reflect this: In the context of hg smartlog : hg smartlog gives you a focused view of your branches and how they relate to the development trunk. I know Git can produce this kind of UI if you know the incantation, but the critical thing here is not that it can be done; it’s that it becomes the default view of their source-control environment. That is where the power comes from: making it really intuitive for users to use source control and understand the concepts without reading a man page. In the context of hg absorb : hg absorb auto-magically identifies the right commits in a stack to squash fixes into and rewrites history accordingly. This makes it easier to work with stacked changes. This is the type of UI that we need to be inventing for our users: ones that match their intent and do it to the best of their ability, without making the user understand everything they have to do. It’s a little bit magic, but it’s magic in a very clean way. I think a lot of user experiences could benefit from this approach. articles.title: Postgres 19 is late, and it's AI's fault
articles.content: Over the past decade, the timing of PostgreSQL major releases has become very predictable: no earlier than the middle of September, and no later than the middle of October. This year is going to be different. PostgreSQL 19 most likely won’t be released until November, and it’s not impossible that the project could decide to postpone the release further. Moreover, this year, several rather large features were reverted quite late in the beta period: UPDATE/DELETE FOR PORTION OF , SQL Property Graph Queries (SQL/PGQ), and ALTER TABLE … MERGE PARTITION/SPLIT PARTITION were all reverted between August 27 and September 15. While major feature reverts are not especially uncommon immediately after feature freeze, which each year occurs on April 8, it is unusual to see multiple major features get pulled from the release at such a late date. So, what happened? The short answer is that LLMs happened. All software contains bugs, and PostgreSQL’s code base is large, complex, and old. Our git history – converted from CVS – now reaches back more than 30 years, and the first code was written a decade before that. There’s a huge amount of code, and that code contains a huge number of bugs. That’s always been true, and it hasn’t stopped PostgreSQL from being popular or successful. What’s different now is that it’s become vastly easier to find those bugs. Fixing them has also gotten easier, but not to the same degree. Between April 8th, 2025 and September 25, 2025, there were 1037 commits to PostgreSQL’s master branch and 724 commits to REL_18_STABLE . In 2026, during the same date range, there were 1443 commits to the master branch and 1169 commits to REL_19_STABLE . In other words, if you look at the number of commits that went into the master branch only between feature freeze and September 25th, it actually declined slightly from last year to this year, but the number of back-patched commits jumped by more than 60%. It’s possible that some of this jump is the result of committers making more mistakes this year than they did last year, but I don’t think anyone who works on the project really believes that’s the main cause. Rather, it seems likely that PostgreSQL committers were about as conservative in 2026 as they were in preceding years, but a lot more of the mistakes they made were quickly found by LLMs. And it isn’t just mistakes in the latest release. In the same time period, during 2025, there were 248 commits to REL_17_STABLE , and during 2026, there were 433 commits to REL_18_STABLE . In other words, the number of commits being back-patched not just to the release in progress but also to at least one prior release jumped by more than 74% in a single year. The reason for this is simply that a huge number of people on the Internet are now reporting bugs in PostgreSQL that they found using LLMs, and the PostgreSQL committers have been very, very busy fixing them. And I think that’s also why we had so many late reverts, and why the release itself is delayed.
articles.summary: PostgreSQL 19 发布推迟至 11 月，文章称与 AI 热潮导致开发资源紧张有关。

articles.title: Work on GEFS (the Good Enough File System) for OpenBSD progresses
articles.content: Contributed by Peter N. M. Hansteen on 2026-11-01 from the most excellent file shredder dept. As previously reported, Ori Bernstein is working on GEFS, the "Good Enough File System" imported to OpenBSD , and his EuroBSDCon 2026 presentation was very well received. In fact, the video is among the most frequently played from the conference. Now Ori has followed up with more evolved code that includes several important steps towards makin the new file system fit for general use. In a message to tech@ , Ori writes: List: openbsd-tech Subject: Re: GEFS on OpenBSD: A very early preview From: ori () eigenstate ! org Date: 2026-10-31 17:08:42 So, it's probably time for a few updates. First off, thanks to Martijn, and everyone else who tried it out and sent patches. Everything is updated and rebased, and the diff has been regenerated with all of the lastest. I've gone through a the error handling code. In theory the filesystem will handle errors mostly correctly. There are probably still places where theory diverges from reality. I've also forward ported most of the important bugfixes from 9front. The file system now leaves the first FS block unused by default -- we can put disklabels there, which makes it hard to put the superblock there as well. Some userspace tools have been done (you can now mkfs on openbsd!), but snapshot control hasn't. I'm thinking we have a userspace 'gefs' program that lets you handle this, trying to keep the interface similar to the 9front ctl file. The commands below should suffice: gefs debug [0|1] gefs usereserve gefs retain snap timespec gefs snap name newname gefs fork name newname The consistency protocol is still the biggest missing piece; I've been reading the old code for softupdates, since it had the same flavor of problem. what gefs wants, in the ideal case, is some way to put ordering barriers in the commit phases, while still accepting new block i/o, something like the following sequence of steps: 0) normal use, generate dirty blocks and write back in any order. holding mutlk { 1) barrier(), ensure that all blocks written before the commit will be on disk before the commit finishes 2) enqueue free list/deadlist data 3) prepare arena header/footer + superblock } 4) enqueue arena headers 5) barrier() 6) enqueue superblock 7) enqueue arena footers 8) wait for enqueued blocks to hit disk 9) free blocks no longer used by previous gen on 9front, I have a priority queue of blocks that are sorted by (gen, addr) tuples, which means that writes within a generation are flushed to disk as sequentially as they can be, while not crossing generation boundaries. I'm currently thinking I'll implement the same in OpenBSD -- launch syncer kprocs that do synchronous I/O to the block device. If we kick things out of cache and write it back to disk early, that should generally be safe -- The only blocks the buffer cache must not reorder are the arena headers and superblocks, so a flag to pin them unwritten may be all that's needed here.
articles.summary: Ori Bernstein 开发的 OpenBSD 文件系统 GEFS 进展顺利，其在 EuroBSDCon 的演讲广受好评。

articles.title: Stop Hardcoding Your Timeouts
articles.content: A developer rant about tools built for one kind of internet Recently, I’ve been losing my mind to hardcoded timeouts . Silent, arbitrary, unconfigurable time limits baked into tools by developers who apparently have never had to wait more than 200ms for anything in their lives. Let me tell you about my week. The skills Package and the 60-Second Clone Now that coding agents are everywhere, everyone is using skills. The popular way to add them is through packages developed by vercel-labs, and the go-to collection is awesome-copilot , a curated set of skills sitting at 30K+ stars at the time of writing. Except I can’t use it. The repository is too big, and the npx skills installer just chokes and dies. There’s an open issue about this since February #278 on the vercel-labs/skills repo and no one has responded. I’d be happy to send a PR and fix it myself. I just need someone to acknowledge it exists. Is there a configuration option? A --timeout flag? An environment variable? No, there is nothing. The workaround I found? Clone the repo manually first, then install from the local copy. It works, mostly. Except now skills-lock.json points to a path on my machine. My colleagues cannot use it. I also have to update my copy everytime I want update my skills. One workaround creates a lot of other problems. Docker Gordon and the 2-Minute Death Timer Then came Docker Gordon, the AI-powered debugging assistant baked into Docker. Useful concept. I was stepping through a container build issue, the kind that requires iteration: tweak, rebuild, inspect, repeat. I’ve never used Gordon but when the error manifested itself, it came with a suggestion to try Gordon and so I did. Except Gordon has a hard limit: if your container doesn’t finish building within two minutes , it gives up. The session dies. You start over. A two-minute build might sound like plenty if you’re in a fast environment with warm caches and pulled base images. But if you’re pulling a fresh base image over a slower connection? Debugging a multi-stage build with several heavy layers? Forget it. Gordon has already moved on. There is no way to configure this. No GORDON_TIMEOUT=600 env var. No --build-timeout flag. Nothing. The tool just assumes that two minutes is forever, and if you need more, that’s your problem. The Pattern That’s Driving Me Crazy Developers often working on fast machines, in offices or homes with gigabit connections, in cities with world-class infrastructure. They build tools with timeout defaults that reflect their own experience. And then they ship those tools to the whole world, with no knobs to turn. The thing is, timeouts need to exist. Infinite waits are bad. Hanging processes are bad. I’m not arguing against timeouts. I’m arguing against unconfigurable timeouts. Against the implicit message that says: if you can’t do this in 60 seconds, your environment is wrong, not my assumption. A timeout should be: A safe default for the common case Clearly documented so users know it e

articles.title: the lost malloc()
articles.content: The lost malloc() 2026-10-29 (Sorry, I couldn't resist not putting a catchy title :) Prompted by another project idea that popped into my mind, I did some Unix archaeology and looked at the original sources . This is the most fun I've ever had reading someone else's code - probably due to the historical significance. But also because of how delightfully approachable it was, compared to modern monstrocities. This is a short(-ish) post regarding how they handled the mundane and boring task of allocating and managing memory (in C). In the future I'd like to read more about Unix the OS, its design, architecture & implementation. A long time ago... In a PDP far, far away, our journey begins with the fourth edition of Unix, released November '73, more than half a century ago . C actually first appeared in the second edition, released the year before, but wasn't extensively used. V4 is special because even the majority of the kernel was written in (let's call it "medieval") C by that point. The system had grown, however, and it was quite capable. You'll find that many Unix things we have today in POSIX-land were already present in V4. Super fun fact: A tape containing V4 was only found last year ! Previously, it was thought to be completely lost to time. While cleaning a storage room, our staff found this tape containing UNIX v4 from Bell Labs, circa 1973 ~ Rob Ricci Linear allocation The first interesting bit is found among the C "compiler" sources. In quotes, because it wasn't a monolithic compiler as we know it today. Rather, it was a set of distinct tools which you chained in order to get an object file from C code. In /usr/c/c20.c:814 , from what I can gather a very primitive optimiser, if you will (referred to as "C object code improver" in V5; there aren't many comments in V4) you see: alloc(an) { register int n; register char *p; n = an; n++; n =& ~01; if (lasta+n >= lastr) { if (sbrk(2000) == -1) { write(2, "Out of space\n", 14); exit(1); } lastr =+ 2000; } p = lasta; lasta =+ n; return(p); } Isn't that fascinating? This routine is used throughout the program to allocate memory. And if you squint, this is just a linear allocator. It aligns the size, checks if the region is big enough, otherwise tries to extend it. On failure, it just cold-exits. Which means callers don't have to check for NULL every single time, and indeed they do not. The "region" isn't named, unlike how you'd do it today with arenas. However, the above does have a nice property, in that by using sbrk() , when we extend the heap, no pointer is invalidated. And they don't bother freeing memory, because why would they? There's no need. Everything exists for the lifetime of the program. dmr/malloc This is the most interesting bit in my opinion, and the reason why I chose that title. In Dennis' directory, you find a file named malloc.c . And you see two functions there: struct map { char *m_size; char *m_addr; }; malloc(mp, size) struct map *mp; mfree(mp, size, aa) struct map *mp;

articles.title: My reflex of assuming our servers need ever-growing amounts of RAM
articles.content: You're using a tool with a too-generic User-Agent You're probably reading this page because you've attempted to access some part of my blog (Wandering Thoughts) or CSpace , the wiki thing it's part of. Unfortunately whatever you're using to do so has a HTTP User-Agent header value that is too generic or otherwise excessively suspicious. Unfortunately, as of early 2025 there's a plague of high volume crawlers (apparently in part to gather data for LLM training) that behave like this. To reduce the load on Wandering Thoughts I'm experimenting with (attempting to) block all of them, and you've run into this. All HTTP User-Agent headers should clearly identify what they are, and for non-browser user agents, they should identify not just the software involved but also who specifically is using that software. An extremely generic value such as " Go-http-client/1.1 " is not something that I consider acceptable any more. One specific thing is that if your HTTP User-Agent header contains an explicit marker that you are only 'compatible' with what your User-Agent suggests, you must include an explicit, real URL that describes your activities or the software. A minimal HTTP User-Agent such as 'Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; mysoftware)' is not acceptable. The same is true if your HTTP User-Agent says that you are a 'bot' of some sort; your bot needs a working URL explaining itself. An email address is not sufficient in either case. Chris Siebenmann, 2026-04-18

articles.title: My favourite laptop
articles.content: I’m not a big owner of things, but the best laptop I’ve ever owned is a roughed-up 2015 Thinkpad X250. For the flex, here it is running a GUI shell sat on top of the microkernel I’m currently working on (blog post about this incoming… eventually). Here’s a list of things that I think make it brilliant. I don’t want to pretend that any of these things are uniquely exemplary: far from it. It is the confluence of them, and not any one in particular, that makes me love using it. Size It’s pretty tiny. Its form-factor fits snuggly into the footprint of an A4 piece of paper, so it sits alongside books and folders when placed in a small rucksack without risking damage. It weighs almost nothing too: even with the extra capacity battery, it’s only about 1.45 Kg. Light enough that you almost don’t notice it when travelling. Performance Mine has an i5-5200U: 4 logical cores, maxing out at 2.7 GHz. I upgraded it to 8 GB of RAM a while back: more than enough for some light on-the-go programming. Even at full pelt, I’ve never heard the fan kicking up much of a fuss. Now that I think about it, I’m not even certain that it works. Battery The X250 has both an internal battery and an external battery slot. I’ve opted for the largest after-market external battery I could find. When doing casual work the laptop will easily survive for north of 10 hours without a charge, stretching to 12 hours if I’m careful. Repairability The X250 was quite popular and replacement parts retail very cheaply on ebay. It’s not the easiest to disassemble Thinkpad by any means but I can tear it apart entirely with the pocket phillips I keep on my keyring. I have previously replaced: The internal battery The lid camera The keyboard The motherboard Every time you open up a laptop you run the risk of damaging something important either via a slip of the hand or simply the accumulated toll of loosening and tightening dozens of tiny screw threads. Despite that, my X250 has proved remarkably resilient and has never sustained any major damage despite more than more than a dozen tear-downs. Keyboard As with most Thinkpads, the keyboard feels lovely to use. When you spend a lot of time writing code the reliability and sensitivity of a keyboard starts to matter a lot. Coupled with my text editor , the experience of writing code on the thing is beautifully snappy. Operating System I opted for Endeavour OS. In the usual Arch Linux tradition, it favours native package installs over sandboxed applications. As a result my install sits at around 30 GB. A 128 GB M.2 SSD raided from another second-hand machine is more than enough to cover that and everything I’m working on. I’ve slimmed down my systemd setup as much as possible and the thing boots from cold in about 8 seconds. Cost Here’s where the X250 beats out most competition. I bought mine second-hand for about £100 in 2018. They’ve only got cheaper since then. I’m not afraid to take it anywhere because it’s barely worth stealing and would be cheap t

articles.title: vercel-labs/agent-desktop (Rust)
articles.content: Computer use for AI agents: read and operate desktop apps through the OS accessibility tree. A CLI and C library for macOS, Windows and Linux. A snapshot returns JSON with a ref for every element an agent can act on. The agent acts on a ref and snapshots again to check, with no pixel matching; the loop stays in your agent. Every CLI call runs in its own process. Headless calls still prohibit foreground activation and synthesized input. Snapshots, clipboard reads, screenshots, command output and debug artifacts can contain private desktop content. Keep them out of public logs and uploads. The optional JEV helper sends screen descriptions to a configured model provider; it is separate from the native CLI. See privacy and data handling . Install on macOS, Windows or Linux with npm: npm install -g agent-desktop agent-desktop version Bun, Yarn and pnpm can install the same package. It includes native binaries and platform helpers for x64 and ARM64. For direct execution without a JavaScript launcher, download the matching native archive from GitHub Releases and keep its helper beside the executable. Official Homebrew and Scoop packages are being submitted; they are not yet available in the default catalogs. The repository no longer maintains a custom Homebrew tap or Scoop bucket. macOS needs Accessibility permission: agent-desktop permissions --guide . Windows needs no grant for apps at your terminal's integrity level. Linux needs the user's graphical session with at-spi2-core . See installation and permissions for package-manager behavior, release archives, and building from source. Observe, act on a ref, observe again. Any app name from agent-desktop list-apps works; Finder is the macOS example. Each command prints one JSON envelope; a trimmed snapshot follows the commands. agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i # interactive elements, each with a ref agent-desktop click @s8f3k2p9:e8 # act on a ref from that snapshot agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i # observe again to verify { "version" : " 2.6 " , "ok" : true , "command" : " snapshot " , "data" : { "app" : " Finder " , "window" : { "id" : " w-204749 " , "title" : " Downloads " }, "snapshot_id" : " s8f3k2p9 " , "ref_count" : 59 , "complete" : true , "tree" : { "role" : " window " , "name" : " Downloads " , "children" : [ { "role" : " treeitem " , "name" : " Documents " , "ref_id" : " @s8f3k2p9:e8 " , "available_actions" : [ " Click " ] } ] } } } Refs belong to their snapshot. A bare @e8 is rejected with INVALID_ARGS . When the UI changes, an action returns STALE_REF or AMBIGUOUS_TARGET : take a new snapshot and use its refs. Several windows give AMBIGUOUS_TARGET ; snapshot lists the candidate window ids in error.details . Pass one with --window-id . Dense apps: map first with snapshot --skeleton --app Slack -i --compact , then drill into one region with snapshot --root @s8f3k2p9:e3 -i --compact . Headless by default. articles.title: Googling "Zelda" today offers a glimpse of how search worked in 1998
articles.content: The year was 1998. Britney Spears topped the charts, Bill Clinton was impeached, and a couple of little websites called Google and Ars Technica came online. It was also the year Nintendo released The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on the Nintendo 64. Google, which has come to dominate the Internet (Ars is still working on that), is celebrating the imminent release of the Ocarina of Time remaster by temporarily transporting us back to that storied year with a search Easter egg. To access the Google time machine, you just have to search for either “Zelda” or “Ocarina of Time.” Google will load the standard 2026 results page, but you’ll see an animated Master Sword in the lower right corner. It appears on both mobile and desktop—just click the sword and enjoy the show. After a little time-skipping animation and a Link shout (you know the one), you’ll swear it’s 1998 again. The search page is transformed into a simple list of blue links with retro Google branding. This is particularly apt given the time-shifting mechanics in Ocarina of Time . Behold the simplicity of ’90s search. Credit: Google Behold the simplicity of ’90s search. Credit: Google Classic Google used to provide a list of 10 links on each page, but there are only seven included in the Easter egg. This is a curated list of links rather than a real search. You get the official Nintendo Zelda page, Zelda on Wikipedia, Zelda games on Amazon, and a couple more. You can go back to the modern version of Google’s search results at any time by clicking the sword again. Oh, you don’t want to do that? Sadly, this is a very limited experience. The Google of today is much different, and if you try to search for anything from the retro interface, you are immediately booted back to 2026 with all the AI, sponsored content, suggested searches, and social media links. Web links are way down the page in today’s Google search results. Credit: Google Web links are way down the page in today’s Google search results. Credit: Google The Ocarina of Time left its mark on a generation of gamers, and clearly, some of them went on to work at Google. The company’s intention is probably to leverage nostalgia to build hype for Nintendo’s big launch, but there’s also something a little sad about this. Google’s push into generative AI is transforming search in a way that many people don’t like. Seeing the simple, minimalist roots of Google search on display drives home how much the company’s core product has changed. The Ocarina of Time has changed a lot, too. The remastered game has been completely re-created, with slick Switch 2 graphics, modern controls for movement and camera, numerous quality-of-life improvements, and more. The game is available for preorder now at $60 for digital and $70 for physical. It launches on November 5 for Nintendo Switch 2.
articles.summary: 谷歌搜索“Zelda”今日可呈现1998年风格的搜索结果页面，致敬Google与Ars Technica上线及《时之笛》发售之年。
